places.name: Phượng Minh Cung
places.size: A great sect's founding seat on a high ridge: a domain about 4 km across, some 300 members in its day plus servants and mortal families (around 1,500 residents), about 200 buildings. Now the old seat, the sect having moved its court away in 1162, so it is half-staffed and quiet.
places.where: High mountain, 1.68 km up, on the ridges of Thê Ngô Lĩnh in the south. Inland, no coast or river. Metal qi is strongest. Nearest: the ruin Minh Cổ Bảo 79 km, the peak Triều Phượng Đỉnh 112 km. Founded 480 on the empty lands of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung; the sect's court has since moved to Hỏa Ti Trấn. Map crop: a high range of bare grey and snow-whitened crags with dark forest only in the valleys, a river along the north-west edge, a small lake in a southern valley, no sea in view; the seat sits on a crest in the heart of the range.
places.imagined: Early evening after a clear day. A palace of red lacquer climbs a ridge around one colossal wutong tree whose crown stands above the highest roof. The lower halls are swept and lit; the upper courts are dim, their lanterns unlit.
places.subject: The place: Phượng Minh Cung, the old seat of a great fire-and-wood sect, seen from high above its ridge. Setting: a high mountain ridge at about 1,700 metres, steep crags of bare grey and white rock with dark forest only in the folds and the green wutong (ngô đồng) groves confined to the terraces, thin cloud in the valleys below, a long range of bare saw-toothed ridges behind, and a thin river glinting far off in the north-west valley. The palace occupies the whole ridge for about four kilometres, built as a stack of walled terraces climbing toward a summit. About two hundred buildings: red-lacquered halls with golden-brown glazed roofs in two and three tiers, long covered galleries joining terrace to terrace, eight tall pagodas with stacked eaves, gate towers on every wall, and drum and bell towers at the corners. Roads of pale stone zigzag up the face in broad switchbacks. At the summit stands one colossal ancient wutong tree, its trunk as wide as a hall, its great green crown spreading over the highest roof and shading a whole courtyard. Wutong groves cover the lower terraces in neat rows. The lower third is alive: smoke from kitchens, laundry drying on long lines, a few hundred servants, caretakers and mortal families, small carts on the road. The upper courts are quiet and swept but unlit, with empty training yards, and moss softening the roof ridges: the sect has moved its court away and left a hundred caretakers to keep the old seat. Late golden light from the upper left lights the red walls and the tree crown, with long shadows to the lower right. Beyond the walls, wutong orchards are planted in terraced rows of some four thousand young trees, and a pale stone road, wide enough for six carts, runs down the south ridge to the market far below. About a dozen caretaker families live in the gate-village at the foot of the first stair,. The summit tree is hung with a few hundred red silk ribbons that stir slightly in the wind.

places.name: Trúc Thực Viên
places.size: A minor sect of spirit farmers: about 60 people (20 cultivators, 40 field hands), a walled farm-compound about 500 m across with some 45 buildings, plus fields all around, because the sect is young (founded 760) and humble.
places.where: Wet grassland, 30 m above the sea, inland, no river, on a low plain below the bamboo forest Tử Trúc Lâm. Wood qi dominates. A vassal of Phượng Minh Cung, righteous. Nearest: the beast lair Trúc Thử Nguyên 79 km, the village Bích Lãng 152 km. Map crop: a grassy headland of wet green and golden ground, bulging into a blue gulf to the south and east, with a river running down its western side and another in the north; the bamboo forest lies inland to the north-west.
places.imagined: Midday in early autumn, the seed harvest. Terraced beds of tall golden bamboo bow under heavy seed, and long swept earthen floors spread with seed dry in the sun.
places.subject: The place: Trúc Thực Viên, the Garden of the Bamboo Seed, a small farming sect, seen from above a low grassy plain. Setting: a low wet grassland headland with small ponds and drainage ditches, a dark green wall of the bamboo forest along the north edge, a river curling along the west side, and the blue gulf lapping the headland's southern and eastern shore a few kilometres away. The sect is a modest walled compound about five hundred metres across at the centre of its own fields: a low earthen wall, two timber gates, and about forty-five buildings. The central hall is plain, roofed with split bamboo, with a veranda; around it stand six long bamboo-roofed barns, drying sheds, a seed store on stilts, two dormitories, a kitchen yard, and animal pens. Around the compound lie terraced beds of tall golden bamboo, thirty or more, each bowed under heavy tassels of seed, divided by narrow canals. Between the beds are long swept earthen threshing floors, pale and round and rectangular, each spread with drying seed in patterned rows, as many as twenty. Fields of spirit grain in green and amber stripes extend toward the edges. Forty or so field hands with wide hats rake and turn seed, bamboo-pole carts and oxen move on the lanes, a handful of grey-robed cultivators stand over the beds. A flock of long-tailed birds (phoenix-kin) lands on the nearest floors to eat the seed. Soft golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right, warm dust. Two long irrigation canals run from the river through the compound to the beds, each crossed by three small timber bridges. The compound's eastern yard holds a ring of eight round seed-drying platforms, each paved with fitted bamboo slats, where the hulled seed is spread in spirals of pale gold. A rack of long wooden winnowing fans stands against the barn wall, and a line of lidded clay jars, perhaps sixty, holds seed set aside for the beast keepers who come by cart from far along the coast.

places.name: Thiều Âm Thị
places.size: A market town of musicians and instrument makers: about 300 stalls and workshops and 150 houses in a bamboo grove along a river, roughly 700 m long, with perhaps 2,500 people at a busy fair. Small, but busy.
places.where: Bamboo forest on a river at 140 m, inland, at the foot of Phượng Minh's ridges. Metal qi. Opened in 485 by Phượng Minh's founder. Nearest: the peak Minh Cầm Phong 112 km, the ruin Minh Cổ Bảo 146 km. Map crop: a narrow river valley between bare crags with bamboo and green only along the water, a small lake a few kilometres to the east, snowy peaks to the north-west; low forested ridges to the south.
places.imagined: Late afternoon wind. Every lane hung with curtains of bamboo flutes and pipes drying on strings, clicking and whistling. A music stage stands over the water.
places.subject: The place: Thiều Âm Thị, the Market of the Shao Music, a market of instrument-makers, seen from above a river among bamboo groves. Setting: a slow, clear river about fifty metres wide curving down a narrow valley, its banks dense with green bamboo groves, while bare grey-brown crags of the mountain range rise steeply on both sides and a small round lake gleams a little way to the east, the groves opening into a long clearing along the water. The market stretches seven hundred metres along both banks: some three hundred bamboo-roofed stalls and workshops in rows along six lanes, around a hundred and fifty low houses on posts, plank bridges and three arched stone bridges over the river, and wooden quays with moored punts. Every lane is strung overhead with hanging curtains of bamboo flutes, pipes and panpipes drying on lines, so that the lanes shimmer pale green and gold, and long racks of drying bamboo canes stand in the open. At the heart of the market a large raised stage of lacquered wood roofed in tile stands out over the water on piles, with tiered seating on the bank. Zither makers, drum-skin stretchers, lacquer workshops with red-painted drums stacked in pyramids: each trade has its own lane. The crowd is dense: musicians in bright robes, buyers from far towns, porters with flutes in bundles, rafts of cut bamboo drifting down. Wind turns the hanging pipes. Light comes from the upper left, soft and golden, with long shadows. The craftsmen's houses are two storeys, with workshops below and sleeping lofts above; the lacquer lane smells of resin and is lined with open jars of red and black. At the upstream end a log-boom holds back floating bamboo canes while cutters strip them. Notes of a dozen instruments overlap across the water, and a procession of performers in saffron and white robes crosses the middle bridge toward the stage with pipes raised, a hundred figures at most.

places.name: Mạch Điền Trấn
places.size: A walled granary town of about 3,000 roofs and perhaps 12,000 people, wall about 1.2 km across, one great granary at its centre, because it feeds a great sect's palace.
places.where: Flat grassland at sea level on the coast where a river meets the gulf. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the hot springs Hải Ôn Tuyền 90 km, Noãn Ba Tuyền 103 km. Map crop: a river reaching a blue gulf bay at the town, flanked by green and gold rolling hills and forest to the west; the valley mouth opens southward onto the bay, and a ridge of grey rock stands at the south-west edge.
places.imagined: Harvest time, low sun. Wheat barges tie up at a timber quay under a huge granary raised on mushroom-shaped stones.
places.subject: The place: Mạch Điền Trấn, Wheat Fields Town, seen from above a coastal valley mouth between rolling hills. Setting: a broad valley floor of ripe wheat in golden squares and strips, divided by irrigation ditches and tree-lined lanes, shut in by low green hills and forest on the west and opening to the blue gulf bay on the south; a wide brown river reaches the sea through a muddy delta with sandbars. The town sits where river meets sea, enclosed by a squared grey stone wall about a kilometre and a quarter across with four gates and corner towers, a moat fed from the river. Inside are around three thousand tile and thatch roofs in tight lanes, a market square, mills with turning wheels on the river, and bakeries with chimneys. At the centre stands one tall granary, many times taller than the houses, raised on a ring of dozens of mushroom-shaped staddle stones, its steep thatched roof the highest thing on the plain, with a spiral ramp running up to a loading door. Smaller granaries with thatch cluster around it. Outside the wall a timber quay stretches along the river, with a dozen wheat barges tied up and being loaded by lines of porters, and a long cart road running inland across the wheat. Harvesters in the fields, haystacks in long rows, ox-carts. Golden low light from the upper left, long soft shadows, dust over the threshing floors. Four tide-mills on the river turn heavy stones, and six long drying sheds hold sacks in stacked rows. A second row of lesser granaries, twelve in number, stands outside the east gate, each on its own ring of staddle stones. Barge captains in blue jackets haggle at the quay, a customs clerk counts sacks with a tally rod, and a ferry crosses the river mouth to a small shrine on the far spit.

places.name: Thanh Khê Thành
places.size: A port city: a walled grid about 3 km across holding some 20,000 roofs and perhaps 90,000 people, with a harbour wall about 2 km long, because it is the great sect's gulf port.
places.where: Flat grassland at sea level on the coast, a brook meeting the gulf, river present. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung, founded by it in 560. Nearest: the forest Kim Trúc Lâm 79 km. Map crop: a narrow strip of forested coast between green hills and a big blue gulf; mountains of grey rock rise further inland to the west, a small brook enters the sea at the city, and a headland shows at the top of the crop.
places.imagined: Dusk. A glowing line of thousands of red lanterns along the whole harbour wall, seen from out at sea.
places.subject: The place: Thanh Khê Thành, Clear Brook City, seen from above and slightly out to sea, at dusk. Setting: a narrow strip of green forested hills falling to a deep blue gulf, bare grey mountains rising far inland behind, and a clear brook that winds down a small valley and enters the harbour through a stone sluice. The city is a walled grid about three kilometres across: a grey stone wall with eight gate towers, straight avenues, twenty thousand grey-tiled roofs in dense blocks, a large central market square, canals, temple compounds with green roofs, shipyards with ships on slips, warehouses in long rows near the water. A wide curved harbour basin is closed by a great harbour wall two kilometres long with two lighthouse towers. All along the top of the harbour wall hangs an unbroken row of red lanterns, thousands of them, lit, so the wall glows as a red line on the water, and their reflections run across the harbour. In the basin lie some sixty ships: trading junks with square sails, fishing boats, and a few big sea-going ships with painted eyes at the bow, with lighters moving between them. Quays crowded with porters and carts. Beyond the wall small lanterns float on the water. The sky is deep violet-gold with the last sun from the upper left on the grey roofs, and tiny figures walk the lantern wall. Beyond the south wall are the fishing quarter, with drying nets, a shipyard where three hulls stand on slips, and an oil store. Forty harbour pilots live in a row of tall narrow houses by the lighthouse. At the foot of every lantern post sits a tiny shrine of red clay, and families come along the wall at dusk carrying a lantern each, a slow chain of lights, tiny figures, lit one by one from the last.

places.name: Đào Khê Thôn
places.size: A small village of about 35 houses and 150 people, with orchards and fields, sitting at the edge of a ruined platform about 400 m across.
places.where: Grassland at 10 m, inland, with a brook, below the ridges. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Beside the ruined palace grounds of the fallen Cửu Thiều Cung. Nearest: the hot spring Đào Hoa Thang 75 km. Map crop: a river running east across rolling green hills, with forest on the slopes and an orange autumn patch to the north-west, bare crags to the south; a bay of the sea shows at the lower-right edge.
places.imagined: Spring, peach blossom. A village hugs the edge of a great terraced platform where wild peach trees grow out of cracks in old paving slabs.
places.subject: The place: Đào Khê Thôn, Peach Brook Village, seen from above. Setting: gentle rolling green hills with dark forest on their slopes, bare crags far to the south, and a clear brook widening into a small river that runs across the picture toward a bay of the sea at the lower-right corner. The village lies at the edge of a huge terraced stone platform, once the palace grounds of a fallen sect, now overgrown. The platform is about four hundred metres across, in three broad stepped terraces of pale weathered paving slabs, cracked and tilted, with rows of broken stone column bases standing in lines like a forest of stumps, a ruined broad stair, and the footprint of a great hall marked by a ring of foundation stones. Wild peach trees in full pink-white blossom grow straight out of the cracks between slabs, dozens of them, with fallen petals pooling pink on the stone. Around one corner of the platform stand about thirty-five small houses with grey tile roofs, courtyards, drying racks and vegetable plots, a well, a footbridge over the brook, and a few small fields and a peach orchard in rows. Nobody has cut a tree or lifted a slab: the houses stop exactly at the platform edge. A few villagers pick peaches into baskets, and children play on the broken columns. Soft golden light from the upper left, long shadows across the stone, quiet and grief-touched. Three terraces step down toward the brook, each about forty metres deep, and the lowest holds a worn square basin where a fountain once stood. Wild peach seedlings sprout along every seam. A grass-grown cart road skirts the platform without touching it. The villagers' houses are built of salvaged brick from outside the platform, never from its stone. Each household keeps a small plot of beans, and there is a communal well at the point where the first house meets the first column base.

places.name: Hà Loan Thôn
places.size: A stilt village of about 40 houses and 180 people on a river bend, with plank walks and boats.
places.where: Grassland at 10 m, inland on a wide river bend, which floods every autumn. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the hot spring Noãn Ba Tuyền 125 km, the town Mạch Điền 180 km. Map crop: a wide river looping through green rolling hills with forest pockets, a blue bay of the sea about a hundred kilometres to the south-east, bare crags at the lower left.
places.imagined: Early autumn, the river rising, boats tied under the houses.
places.subject: The place: Hà Loan Thôn, River Bend Village, seen from above a broad floodplain. Setting: a wide, slow brown-green river bends in a great loop across a low valley of reeds and pasture between rolling green hills, heading toward a bay of the sea beyond, with side channels, sand banks, and willows; the far horizon is hazy. At the inside of the bend stand about forty timber houses, every one raised high on tall stilts above the floodplain, with steep thatched roofs and open verandas, their undersides dark and open. The houses are joined by a network of plank walkways and rope bridges, some two hundred metres of boardwalk, with ladders to the ground. Beneath and between the houses long boats are tied up, perhaps thirty: narrow punts, fish-boats and flat cargo boats, ready for the rising water. A raised timber platform serves as the village square with a small shrine to the river; fishing nets are spread on racks; stacks of reed bundles dry on the bank. Small fields of rice and vegetable plots lie on a slightly raised mound behind, and a herd of buffalo grazes at the edge. The water already laps at some of the lower stilts, a thin brown line high on the posts marking past floods. A few villagers pole boats between houses. Soft light from the upper left, mist over the water. Four larger houses at the bend serve as the village's inn, granary, boat-builder's yard and ferry-office, each with a double-height stilt platform. Fifteen flat-bottomed boats, roofed with plaited mats, are lashed in rows under and between the houses, and at least thirty more lie on the sandbank above the stilts. A line of small flags of plain red cloth marks last year's flood on the pole by the ladder. Children dive from the boardwalks into the brown water.

places.name: Bích Lãng Thôn
places.size: A fishing village of about 45 houses and 200 people behind a basket seawall about 600 m long, below sea level.
places.where: Bamboo forest at -40 m (below the gulf), on the coast, with a river. Wood qi. Held by Trúc Thực Viên. Nearest: the forest Tử Trúc Lâm 79 km, Trúc Thực Viên 152 km. Map crop: a river reaching the sea at a small bay on the south-west shore of a blue gulf, with grassy hills inland and a ridge of grey rock far to the north-east.
places.imagined: Winter re-weaving of the wall. Jade-green waves break on the baskets.
places.subject: The place: Bích Lãng Thôn, Jade Waves Village, seen from above the gulf. Setting: a jade-green sea breaks in white lines against a long curved seawall, and behind it a low coastal strip lies below the level of the water, dense with bamboo groves. The seawall is about six hundred metres long, made of great woven bamboo baskets, each the size of a cart, packed with stones and stacked three high in a long curve; crews of men on top re-weave and replace baskets, with piles of fresh-cut bamboo and coils of rope on the landward side. Behind the wall are about forty-five small houses of bamboo and thatch, packed close, with drying racks of fish and nets, salt pans, smoke houses, and boat sheds. A narrow stream runs out through a gated sluice in the wall into a small harbour at one end, with some twenty fishing boats with brown sails and several drawn up on a shingle beach. Bamboo groves crowd the houses in tall green stands, and bamboo scaffolds and stacks of cut poles line the lanes, with a small shrine to the waves with a red roof. Fisherfolk haul nets and women split bamboo. The waves are jade and turquoise, golden light from the upper left lights the basket wall, with long shadows to the lower right. At the river mouth a narrow gated channel lets the stream out through the wall, with a plank bridge across it. Behind the basket wall run two ditches, each with sluices, to keep the low land from filling. Outside the wall, long bamboo fish-weirs in V-shapes reach into the surf. Two weaving sheds, open at the sides, hold men and women plaiting new baskets, and the finished baskets, a hundred or so, stand in towers waiting for the stone gangs. Children tie jade-green ribbons on the first basket of each year.

places.name: Tương Phi Đảo
places.size: A natural island, large on the map (about 150 by 275 km): a long steep ridge of bamboo-covered land, the painting showing the north end and a long stretch of the coast; no roof, no landing, no people.
places.where: Bamboo forest, 180 m high, a small steep island off the coast, no river. Water qi. No holder. Nearest: the mine Thạch Thanh Khoáng 230 km, the peak Lâm Hải Nhai 301 km. The legend of the two weeping consorts. Map crop: an elongated island of steep green and grey land standing alone in a wide blue sea, about 150 km across and some 275 km long on the map, with grassy mainland coast far to the north-west; the rocky spine is grey, the flanks green.
places.imagined: Dusk, silent water. Dense bamboo flecked purple-brown to the rocks, like old tear stains.
places.subject: The place: Tương Phi Đảo, the Isle of the Xiang Consorts, a great steep island seen from above the sea at dusk. Setting: a calm blue-grey sea with long swells, a far low coast faint on the horizon. The island is huge, a long ridge-backed land about a hundred and fifty kilometres wide and running off the frame to the south, its spine a line of bare grey rock crests, with every flank, gully and headland below covered in dense bamboo from the waterline to the rock. The canes are flecked with purple-brown spots, like old tear stains, so the whole island looks mottled green and plum, with feathery tops moving in waves in the wind, and a band of paler new shoots along the lower slopes. There is no beach and no landing, only black wave-cut rocks, ledges, stacks, and small sea caves where the bamboo comes right down to the surf; narrow white lines of surf trace the shore for hundreds of kilometres. Thin mist threads along ravines, and from some ravines silver streams fall straight into the sea. Smaller bamboo islets stand off the north cape. No roof, no path, no shrine; far out, a single tiny boat passes at a respectful distance with a bowing figure, to show the scale, and a second drifts further off. The bamboo crowns catch the last gold light from the upper left, with long violet shadows toward the lower right over the water. A sense of mourning, quiet and untouched growth.

places.name: Đan Sơn Mạch
places.size: A natural mountain flank about 6 km long, with a glowing seam about 3 km, with a few ruined watch platforms and a small guard post (about 30 guards).
places.where: High mountain at 1.34 km, inland. Metal qi. Held by Phượng Minh Cung, its spirit vein near its border with the heart, 3 tiles from Thiên Xu's border. Nearest: the peak Quy Vũ Lĩnh 90 km, the mine Đan Sa Quật 135 km. Map crop: a rugged grey mountain range with rust-orange ridges at the south-west, a forest patch beside it, a blue bay of the sea to the north-east about a hundred kilometres away; no river, only a small lake in the north-west.
places.imagined: Dusk. A long seam in vermilion rock glows crimson.
places.subject: The place: Đan Sơn Mạch, the Vein of the Cinnabar Mountain, a spirit vein seen from above and slightly to one side. Setting: a steep mountain flank about six kilometres long, of bare vermilion and rust-red rock among jagged grey ridges, with a far glint of the sea in the north-east and scree fans below and thin pines and pale grass lower down, other dry ridges beyond. A long seam splits the rock along its length for about three kilometres, a jagged crack with glowing edges that burns a deeper crimson at dusk as if molten, where the vein's qi runs close to the surface, with faint wisps of heat shimmering above it and small side-cracks branching out like roots. Along the ridge above stand the scorched stone footings of watch platforms from the last war: a dozen square black-stained stone bases, a broken wall, a fallen gate, collapsed stairs, and scattered blackened beams. Below the ridge a small stone guard post with a red-tiled roof and a walled yard, a signal tower, and a zigzag track keep watch, about thirty guards visible as specks in red-brown cloaks and a column of mules carrying supplies. Alchemists' small camps with tents lie further down the scree. Warm light from the upper left lights the red slope, deep shadows fill the hollows. Scorched stone footings are laid out in a line of nine, each four metres square, with split posts of black timber still upright at two. The seam's brightest section is a gash about forty metres across at the centre, rimmed with glassy red crust, and the guard path hugs the ridge a hundred metres above it. Mules carry sacks of cinnabar down a switchback track, each mule roped to the next; the longest train has twenty animals. A second small camp of alchemists' tents stands beside a spring at the foot of the scree.

places.name: Cao Cương Phong
places.size: A sacred summit: the peak about 2.5 km high, a flat crest about 150 m across, with one stone pillar and nothing else.
places.where: High mountain, 2.56 km up, inland, no river. Metal qi. No holder. A sacred summit (Light): the ode where the phoenix sings on the high ridge. Nearest: the mine Đan Hoàng Quật 146 km, the lava vent Niết Hỏa Khẩu 152 km. Map crop: a jagged mountain spine near the sea: a bay of the sea lies to the north-west beyond the ridge, a dark volcanic cone about a hundred kilometres to the south, green forest on the north-east flank with a thin river down it, grass-covered hills to the west.
places.imagined: First dawn light touching only the crest, pale gold, above a sea of cloud and the wutong hills.
places.subject: The place: Cao Cương Phong, the Peak of the High Ridge, seen from above in the first light of dawn. Setting: a high bare ridge-top above the dark green wutong hills, rising steeply out of a sea of white cloud that fills every valley, with other lower ridges as dark islands in the cloud, the true sea a pale strip far to the north-west and a dark volcanic cone smoking faintly far to the south. The summit ends in a flat crest of pale gold stone about a hundred and fifty metres across, smooth and wind-polished, which is the only part of the mountain yet touched by the sun, glowing bright gold while everything below is still blue and violet in shadow. On the crest stands a single stone pillar, as tall as a house, worn at its top into the shape of a perch, with a long thin shadow. Nothing else is there: no building, no offering, no flag. A single narrow pilgrim path zigzags up the last slope from the cloud, a thread of pale scratches, with a few tiny figures in robes, a dozen at most, climbing in a line to watch the dawn, one standing alone by the pillar. The ridge below is rock and thin alpine grass, with a few twisted pines. Long cold shadows fall to the lower right, with the first golden light from the upper left. A feeling of height and stillness. The crest's gold stone is cut by a single shallow groove about forty metres long where the dawn-pilgrims stand, worn smooth by generations of feet. The perch pillar is eleven metres high, and its top has been worn hollow like a cup that holds dew. The pilgrim path begins at a stone cairn on the forest line and climbs in two hundred and sixty zigzags; at the third turn there is a bare ledge with a pile of pebbles left by travellers who turned back. Sunrise lifts the rim of cloud as a gold ridge.

places.name: Huyền Viên Lâm
places.size: A jungle about 20 km across held by dark apes: several hundred apes in troops, with sleeping platforms in the strangler figs; no human buildings, only a few gatherers' offering stones at the edge.
places.where: Jungle at 450 m, inland, below the wutong hills of Thê Ngô Lĩnh. Wood qi. No holder: held by dark apes. Resource: beast bone. Nearest: the ruin Ẩn Phàm Trại 90 km, the spirit vein Ngô Căn Mạch 168 km. Map crop: a dense dark jungle on a headland by the sea, a bay to the south, a volcanic crater among crags to the north-east, a river curling along the western edge, and grass-hills to the north.
places.imagined: Morning mist in the canopy. Huge strangler figs rise above the roof of jungle, crowns knotted with woven platforms.
places.subject: The place: Huyền Viên Lâm, the Dark Ape Forest, seen from high above a vast jungle. Setting: a dense, unbroken canopy of jungle in many greens, rolling over low hills, with a winding river half-hidden under leaves along its western side, mist drifting in the hollows, a bay of the sea showing blue at the southern edge, and grey crags with a dark crater rising far to the north-east. Above the general canopy rise dozens of enormous strangler figs, each a tower of tangled roots and branches, their crowns knotted with the dark apes' woven sleeping platforms of branch and vine, great round nests hung in clusters, some thirty to fifty nests in each crown, with rope-like vine bridges joining the figs. Dark-furred apes, large as men, sit and swing on the platforms and cross the vine bridges, tiny black shapes; one troop crosses a clearing, and there are heaps of thrown stones and gnawed bone at the foot of two figs. A bare patch of trampled earth marks a gathering ground. At the forest edge, nearest the viewer, a single small cairn with fruit on it stands where gatherers leave offerings, and a tiny herb-gatherer retreats along a path. Fallen trees block one of the paths into the forest. Soft morning light from the upper left, shafts through mist, long shadows. Rope-and-vine bridges run between the figs for nearly two kilometres in one chain, with the apes crossing at a lope. The ground beneath the nests is a litter of fruit stones and bones, and rival troops mark their ranges with piles of smooth river stones, each pile the height of a man's knee. In the east a wide clearing, fallen where a great fig toppled, is heavily trampled, and two lines of apes face each other across it. The herb-gatherers' offering cairn bears a few rotting mangoes.

places.name: Niết Hỏa Khẩu
places.size: A volcanic vent crater about 400 m across on a mountain slope, with a ring of burned stumps about 2 km wide; a few small tents of fire cultivators.
places.where: Volcano slope at 1.76 km, inland. Fire qi. Held by Phượng Minh Cung. Resource: earth-fire essence (địa hỏa tinh). The wutong hills where the phoenix is reborn in fire. Nearest: the peak Thải Phượng Phong 75 km, the peak Cao Cương Phong 152 km. Map crop: a dark volcanic crater in the middle of a grey rock range, with a bay of the sea to the south and another to the north-west, green forest and grass hills to the east and west.
places.imagined: Dusk, heat shimmer over the mouth, fresh green shoots on charred wutong stumps.
places.subject: The place: Niết Hỏa Khẩu, the Nirvana Fire Vent, seen from above a volcanic slope. Setting: a great black-ashed cone amid bare grey rock ridges that radiate from it, with the green wutong forest on the lower slopes east and west and a bay of the sea glinting to the south. In the middle of the slope a fire vent opens as a rough round crater about four hundred metres across, its inner walls glowing orange and red, with a lake of slow-moving molten rock at the bottom crusted in black, and heat shimmer rising above it, thin smoke drifting uphill. The black ash around the mouth is pale grey-warm and lightly steaming. A great ring of burned wutong stumps surrounds the vent, hundreds of charred trunks as thick as pillars, and from nearly all of them fresh bright green shoots and leaves have sprouted out of the black, so the ring glows green against the black ash. A few outbursts have laid dark tongues of cooled lava downhill. On a ledge at the safe edge stand three small tents and a stone hearth where fire cultivators come to temper their arts, with a dozen tiny red-robed figures seated cross-legged facing the vent, and a goat-track path coming up. Dusk light from the upper left, glow of the vent on the underside of the smoke. Three lava tongues, the longest nearly a kilometre, have cooled into black shining ropes across the ash. A single stone staircase of one hundred and eight steps leads up the western side to the tents' ledge, and a line of cairns marks the safe path around the rim. The wutong ring is replanted by the sect each year: new saplings stand in a tidy row a hundred metres outside the stumps, tied to stakes. At the lip a brazier burns constantly, and a cultivator rakes embers into a clay jar to take away.

places.name: Lôi Ngô Lâm
places.size: A wood of tall wutong about 8 km across, several thousand trees, no buildings but a gatherers' shelter.
places.where: Lowland jungle at 20 m, inland, under the storm peaks of Thê Ngô Lĩnh. Water qi. Held by Phượng Minh Cung. Resource: thunder-struck wood (lôi kích mộc). Nearest: the village Lôi Hậu 127 km, the village Lô Châu 168 km. Map crop: a green headland on the coast, jutting north into the blue sea with a wooded island off its north-west, grey rock mountains to the south-west, a river winding down its eastern flank, and a forested coast stretching away east.
places.imagined: A storm clearing. Split wutong trees still green at the top, streaked with white burn scars, glassy fused sand between.
places.subject: The place: Lôi Ngô Lâm, the Thunder-Struck Wutong Wood, seen from above the lowland jungle at the end of a storm. Setting: a low green headland of jungle and grass jutting into the sea with a wooded island offshore, dark thunderclouds still piled on the bare grey storm peaks behind to the south-west and a shaft of low gold light breaking through. The wood is an area about eight kilometres across of tall wutong trees standing a little apart from each other, thousands of them, each with a broad green crown, and a large number are split from crown to root, trunks streaked with white burn scars and black splits, some with half the crown blasted away while the rest still lives. Fallen trunks lie in tangles among them. The ground between the trees is bare grey sand in places, littered with fused, glassy sand in pale green and white blobs and branched fulgurite shapes, shining in the light, and shallow rain pools reflect the sky. A few lightning bolts hang as thin white lines in the far sky over the peaks. A small open gatherers' shelter of poles and thatch stands at the edge of the wood with a stack of fallen wood, and two tiny figures carry a long pale beam out of the trees. Steam lifts off the wet ground. Light from the upper left, long shadows. The shelter has a roof of split wutong shingles and a wall hung with rows of numbered pegs where gatherers hang their coats before entering. Three heaps of fallen wood, sorted by length, wait beside it for the instrument makers' cart, and the roadside is marked by two painted posts. On the headland's tip, three lightning rods taller than the trees stand in a triangle, set by the palace to draw strikes away from the shelter. A small flock of white egrets stands in a rain pool among the fused sand.

places.name: Đào Hoa Thang
places.size: A hot spring pool complex about 300 m across, with steam and peach trees, and a hermit's hut or two (about 6 buildings).
places.where: Grassland at 260 m, inland, no river. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. A hermit's abode. Nearest: the village Đào Khê 75 km, the minor seat Bách Vũ Các 160 km. Map crop: a green grass-and-forest hillside inside the bow of a horseshoe arc of dark forest, with bare rocky mountains to the south and a river curling across the north; a blue bay of the sea lies at the south-east edge about a hundred kilometres away, with orange hills in the north-west.
places.imagined: Early morning. Pink peach blossom floating on blue-white steaming pools.
places.subject: The place: Đào Hoa Thang, the Peach Blossom Hot Spring, seen from above a rolling green grassland. Setting: a soft grassy hillside inside the bow of a dark horseshoe of forest, with grey rocky crags rising to the south, a winding river across the north, and a blue bay of the sea faint at the south-east. The spring forms a series of nine stepped pools down a gentle slope, each a different shade from milky turquoise to pale green to clear blue, edged with white mineral crust, linked by little cascades, about three hundred metres from top to bottom, with veils of white steam lifting from them and drifting in the breeze. Around the pools grows a grove of some sixty peach trees in full pink blossom, and petals float in drifts on the water and gather in pink rafts in the corners. A rough stone-flag path winds between pools. At the lower end sit a few small thatched huts: a hermit's abode with a little garden, a drying rack, a stone table under a tree, and a hot-water channel to a wooden bath, about six buildings in all. Two tiny figures sit by the upper pool in robes. Early morning light from the upper left, gold on the blossom and steam, long shadows to the lower right. The top pool is nearly white, the colour of milk; the second, jade; the third, a steely blue that darkens with depth; the lowest, clear enough to count the stones on its floor. Between them run plank footbridges only a metre wide, and a water-wheel at the second cascade turns a prayer wheel of bamboo. Peach petals drift in rafts of pink to a small drain at the lowest pool. The hermit's garden grows mint, ginger and a single plum tree; a kettle hangs over a fire, and a folding screen of painted paper stands beside the bath.

places.name: Bách Vũ Các
places.size: A minor sect of bird-keepers: about 35 people and some 400 birds; a jungle clearing about 300 m across with about 25 buildings, because it is young (founded 1110) and small.
places.where: Jungle at 40 m, inland, a clearing below the wutong hills of Thê Ngô Lĩnh. Wood qi. A vassal of Phượng Minh Cung, righteous. Nearest: the village Nhục Quế 127 km, the village Hà Loan 160 km. Map crop: a jungle clearing just north of a horseshoe arc of dark forest, with a river across the north, a blue bay of the sea to the east, grey rocky mountains to the south-west and orange hills in the north-east.
places.imagined: Morning, hundreds of birds in the air over a jungle clearing, tall bird lofts on pillars.
places.subject: The place: Bách Vũ Các, the Pavilion of a Hundred Feathers, a small sect of bird-keepers, seen from above a jungle clearing. Setting: dense green jungle on three sides with tall wutong crowns and a horseshoe of dark forest to the south, the clearing about three hundred metres across, a small stream crossing it, a river glinting beyond to the north, and a blue bay of the sea at the far eastern edge. The compound is about twenty-five buildings of pale timber with green tile and thatch roofs: a long main hall with an upturned roof, three round dormitories, a kitchen, a medicine hut, and a feed store. Its signature is the bird lofts: eight tall timber towers on pillars, each three to five storeys with latticed walls and perches along each floor, one tower far taller than the others, rising above the treetops, plus a long aviary hall with a roof of netting and several domed cages. Hundreds of birds, around four hundred, fill the air above: flocks of white cranes, long-tailed pheasants, brightly coloured parrots and messenger birds circling the towers in loose spirals, with feathers drifting down. Raised perches line the courtyard, and a training ring where a few thirty-five or so disciples in green robes hold out arms with birds, tiny figures. Paths of beaten earth lead into the jungle. Golden light from the upper left through the mist. The tallest bird loft stands twelve storeys and holds the messenger pigeons, each compartment numbered by a coloured thread tied to the lattice. A wooden catapult of strips and counterweights launches birds in training. The kitchen yard has long tables of feed grain in baskets, and by the stream stands a sorting shed where feathers are graded by colour into sixteen bins. In the middle of the yard a stone ring ten metres across is raked smooth for the morning counts, and a young disciple holds up a tally slate.

places.name: Tử Trúc Lâm
places.size: A bamboo forest about 15 km across with a woodcutters' track and a few bamboo huts; no settlement.
places.where: Bamboo forest at 100 m, inland near the coast. Wood qi. No holder. Nearest: the village Bích Lãng 79 km, the ruin Trúc Địch Viện 146 km. Purple bamboo. Map crop: a wide forest on rolling hills just inland of a blue gulf, with a bay-coast to the south, a bright clearing and open meadow at the centre, rivers running down both sides to the shore, and grey crags at the north-west.
places.imagined: Morning mist. Dense groves of dark purple bamboo, with golden light in the aisles.
places.subject: The place: Tử Trúc Lâm, the Purple Bamboo Forest, seen from above. Setting: a vast low forest of dense bamboo covering rolling lowland hills, in which the canes are a dark glossy purple-black, so the whole forest appears as a deep plum-green sea with feathery crowns, with silver streams winding down both flanks toward the blue gulf that closes the picture to the south, mist lying in hollows, and a bright green meadow opening in the middle. Within the forest there are lighter pockets where a stand of bamboo has flowered and gone gold and where young shoots come up in vivid pale green. A few straight lanes of cleared aisles cut through for harvest, light falling gold into them from the upper left, and a narrow cart track runs in along a stream to a small woodcutters' camp of four or five bamboo huts with a bamboo-pole drying yard and stacked purple poles, and a raft of cut canes on the stream. Three or four tiny figures in conical hats carry bundles. A single pale stone shrine marks a clearing deep in the forest. Birds fly low over the crowns, a thin column of cooking smoke rises, and the whole picture is hushed and cool. Long soft shadows to the lower right. Harvested aisles are marked with stripes of pale stumps, each about the length of a stride. The woodcutters' camp is a ring of five huts around a fire pit, with a long rack of cut purple poles in stacks of fifty and a covered raft moored at the stream bend. In one cut aisle a procession of eleven bearers carries a single enormous canopy pole, forty metres long, on their shoulders in single file. The shrine in the forest is a ring of seven standing stones about a metre high, bound with faded purple cloth.

places.name: Minh Cầm Phong
places.size: A mountain peak about 900 m high and 4 km across at its base, with a hermit's hut (one or two buildings) on a ledge.
places.where: High mountain at 910 m, inland. Metal qi. No holder; a hermit's abode (A-5). Nearest: the peak Phượng Dực Phong 79 km, the market Thiều Âm Thị 112 km. Map crop: a jagged peak among bare grey crags with snow in the high gullies, a river curling down a valley to the south-west and a green forested valley beyond; no sea in view.
places.imagined: Evening, a lone peak above bamboo, wind making the rocks hum.
places.subject: The place: Minh Cầm Phong, the Peak of the Singing Zither, seen from above. Setting: a solitary steep peak rising nine hundred metres out of bare grey crags in a range of snow-streaked ridges, with bamboo groves filling the lower valleys and a clear river curling away to the south-west. The peak is a narrow crest of grey-gold fluted rock, its flanks scored with long vertical grooves like the strings of a zither, wind-carved stone ribs in parallel, with tufts of grass and twisted pine in the cracks and a cap of pale stone at the top. Bamboo climbs the lower slopes in a dark green skirt, with pockets of snow lingering in the upper gullies, with thin streams falling in white ribbons down the grooves. On a ledge about two-thirds of the way up, sheltered under an overhang, sits a single hermit's hut with a thatched roof, a small terrace garden, a drying rack and a stone table, with one tiny figure seated playing a long zither facing the valley. A single thin footpath winds up from the bamboo. Wind trails of cloud stream from the summit. Soft golden evening light from the upper left on the stone ribs, with long blue shadows to the lower right. The grooves are of three kinds: long straight ones a hand deep, thin braided ones like hair, and wide shallow ones that hold small pools after rain; on windy days the whole face sings in a chord of three notes. A rope ladder of bamboo hangs on the last forty metres to the hermit's ledge. The hut is only four metres square, with a stone chimney, a rain barrel and a drying line of herbs, and a carved zither case propped beside the door. A goat browses on the ledge. In the valley below a bamboo-cutters' village sends one thin thread of smoke.
